description: PANTHERA is a multidisciplinary team in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, building FIREWATCH 360, an intelligent platform harmonising NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data to uncover seasonal patterns, detect anomalous burning activity and support environmental decision-making. Based in Nigeria, designed for global scale. Seeking: Python developers, remote sensing analysts, GIS specialists, web developers, data viz designers and science communicators.
summary:
FIREWATCH 360 is a sensor-aware satellite fire intelligence platform designed to make satellite-detected fire activity easier to analyse, compare and understand. It integrates observations from four satellite platforms — MODIS, NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and Suomi-NPP — while accounting for differences in their spatial resolutions, observation characteristics and confidence classifications. Rather than simply merging all observations, FIREWATCH 360 brings them into a common analytical framework while retaining their sensor identities for meaningful comparison.

The project examines spatial patterns, cross-sensor agreement, fire radiative power and historical burning activity. Its Benue State 2024 case study demonstrates the analytical approach, while its Nigeria-wide interactive map extends the platform's geographical perspective through visualisation, filtering and historical activity analysis.

By transforming multiple satellite observations into more connected and interpretable information, FIREWATCH 360 aims to support researchers, environmental stakeholders and decision-makers in understanding fire activity and identifying areas that may warrant further investigation.
details:
FIREWATCH 360: A Sensor-Aware Satellite Fire Intelligence and Historical Burning Activity Platform

Project Overview

FIREWATCH 360 is a geospatial intelligence platform designed to improve how satellite-detected fire activity is organised, compared, visualised and understood. It addresses a significant challenge in satellite fire monitoring: observations from different satellite instruments vary in spatial resolution, observation characteristics, acquisition times and confidence classifications. Simply combining these observations can obscure important differences and lead to misleading interpretations.

Our solution integrates observations from four satellite platforms: MODIS, NOAA-20 VIIRS, NOAA-21 VIIRS and Suomi-NPP VIIRS. Rather than treating every detection as identical, FIREWATCH 360 retains the distinction between satellite sources while organising observations within a common analytical framework. This enables more meaningful spatial and temporal comparisons without assuming that different sensors are interchangeable.

How It Works and Key Features

The project has two complementary components: a detailed 2024 Benue State case study and a Nigeria-wide interactive geospatial platform.

1. Multi-Sensor Harmonisation: FIREWATCH 360 brings observations from four satellite platforms into a common analytical framework using a 1 km-equivalent reference grid. It accounts for differences in sensor characteristics and enables users to examine observations collectively while retaining information about their originating platforms.

2. Interactive Geospatial Explorer: The Nigeria-wide platform provides a geographical interface for exploring satellite-detected fire activity. Users can visualise observations, examine their spatial distribution and interact with the mapped information.

3. Sensor and Confidence Filtering: Users can filter observations by sensor origin, including MODIS, VIIRS or all available sources, and examine confidence classifications. These controls allow more focused exploration of the observations and their characteristics.

4. Harmonised Fire Radiative Power Analysis: The platform incorporates Fire Radiative Power (FRP), expressed in megawatts, as an indicator of the rate of radiant energy released by detected thermal anomalies. A minimum harmonised FRP filter allows users to explore observations according to a selected threshold.

5. Historical Activity Analysis: FIREWATCH 360 includes monthly and annual activity visualisations to help users explore changes in satellite-detected fire activity over time. Its annual chart presents activity against a 2001–2025 historical reference band, showing the baseline mean and ±1 standard deviation range.

6. Spatial and Temporal Pattern Analysis: The analytical workflow organises observations by geographical grid and observation date, allowing examination of active grid cells, recurring activity, cross-sensor agreement and candidate spatial hotspot clusters.

7. Story Mode and Data Exploration: The interactive application combines geographical visualisation with explanatory storytelling, helping users interpret the information rather than simply viewing a collection of satellite points.

Key Results and Metrics

Our 2024 Benue State case study processed:

  • 91,658 raw satellite detections from four satellite platforms.
  • 56,459 harmonised grid-cell observation-days.
  • 22,117 unique active grid cells.
  • 34,431 candidate spatial hotspot clusters, including 10,886 multi-cell clusters.
  • Approximately 67.9% of active grid cells had observations from at least two satellite platforms.

These measurements represent different stages and forms of analysis; harmonised observation-days, active grid cells and candidate clusters should not be interpreted as counts of individual fires.

The Nigeria-wide interactive dashboard also presents selected analytical indicators. Under the displayed filter configuration, its dashboard showed six harmonised hotspots, December 2024 as the peak fire month, a normalised peak value of 2.6, mean radiative power of 50.5 MW, a confidence indicator of 53%, and a selection anomaly of +7.4%, classified as within the normal band.

Its annual historical chart displays a 2026 activity value of 7.1 against a historical mean of 6.9 and an upper reference boundary of 8.8. Since 2026 is not yet complete, this figure must be interpreted as year-to-date activity rather than a completed annual total.

Tools and Technologies

Our development combined satellite data processing, geospatial analysis and interactive application development. Key resources included:

  • NASA FIRMS: Source of MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations.
  • Python: Data processing, organisation and analytical workflows.
  • Google Colab: Computational environment for satellite data analysis.
  • GRID3 and geoBoundaries: Geographical reference and boundary datasets.
  • Geospatial analysis: Spatial filtering, coordinate transformation, grid-based organisation and hotspot pattern analysis.
  • Google AI Studio: Development environment used for the interactive application.
  • Interactive mapping and visualisation: For geographical exploration, filtering and presentation of analytical outputs.

Creativity, Benefits and Intended Impact

The central innovation of FIREWATCH 360 is not the creation of another satellite detection system. It is the effort to make observations from different satellite platforms more meaningfully comparable while preserving their individual characteristics. By combining sensor-aware analysis, spatial organisation, historical context, radiative power indicators and interactive storytelling, the project moves beyond displaying isolated detections towards a more connected understanding of satellite-observed fire activity.

Its intended beneficiaries include researchers, environmental organisations, policymakers, disaster-management institutions and other stakeholders who need to investigate fire activity and its geographical patterns.

Ultimately, FIREWATCH 360 aims to make satellite fire intelligence more accessible and useful for environmental monitoring, research and evidence-informed decision-making. It does not claim to predict or prevent fires; rather, it provides a framework for exploring patterns, identifying areas that may warrant further investigation and supporting a better understanding of fire activity across Nigeria.
